statement.essentials: The branching pattern differs from person to person; the pattern shown first is the simplest, with no cross-links between branches.
statement.anatomy: The branches often join each other in small loops. The patterns have been classified more than once, and no classification describes the variability well.
statement.clinical: In a systematic review using Davis’ classification the commonest pattern was type III (26.8% of 1,497 cases) and the simple type I, the textbook pattern, was only fourth (16.3%). Katz and Catalano’s 100 patients: 24% straight, 14% a loop involving the zygomatic branch, 44% a loop involving the buccal branch, 14% complex, 3% two main trunks. A meta-analysis found a single link between the divisions in 23.1% and two links in 8.9%.

limitations: The classifications of Davis and of Katz and Catalano are not the same, so their percentages cannot be compared type for type. In the model the links are single twigs of typical position, drawn between existing branches; real patterns are more varied.
disagreement: Katz and Catalano found the buccal-loop pattern in 44% of 100 patients, whereas the pooled Davis analysis puts its commonest pattern at 26.8%; the meta-analysis authors conclude that diversity is the rule.
